**The Slowest Goodbye**

The Moon is leaving. Not dramatically—no catastrophe looms—but patiently, at the pace of fingernails growing: roughly 3.8 centimeters each year. It has been drifting away since before anything existed to notice.

We know because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the lunar surface, and we still bounce lasers off them. The light comes back; the distance grows. Four billion years ago, the Moon hung huge in the sky and Earth spun fast enough that a day lasted perhaps six hours. Lunar gravity has been braking our rotation ever since, quietly stretching our days and paying for it with its own orbital energy. Every tide that has ever crept up a beach—the tides that may have nudged life out of the sea and onto land—was part of this slow transaction.

There's something tender about it. The Moon steadied Earth's tilt, gifting us reliable seasons, then spent four billion years receding like a parent slipping out of a room while the child sleeps. Astronomers call it tidal acceleration; poets might call it grace.

One day, billions of years hence, total solar eclipses will end: the Moon will look too small to cover the Sun completely. Future eyes, whatever they belong to, will see only rings of fire where we once watched darkness fall at noon.

Nothing lasts forever, yet everything leaves a trace. The Moon is writing its farewell in tides, and we are lucky enough to read it twice a day.
